summary: A wooden fog-bell tower on the Potomac at Fort Washington, Maryland. The light moved onto it in 1901, and the Coast Guard took the light off it in 2020.

structures.note: 32-foot fog-bell tower per LighthouseFriends; the NPS place page gives 1889.
16-foot replacement tower, 1870; demolished after the light moved to the bell tower in 1901.

access.note: NPS and USLHS: not open to the public. LighthouseFriends: grounds open, tower closed; visitors walk down from the park's parking area to the river bank to see it. The tower stands in Fort Washington Park.

facts.agency: National Park Service (tower in Fort Washington Park)

events.note: Treasury Secretary James Guthrie asked for a light on Digges Point; Secretary of War Jefferson Davis agreed on conditions.
16-foot tower replaced the post, set nearer the water at the end of the wharf. Built at the Lazaretto depot and carried by the tender Tulip, February 1870.
Sixth-order Fresnel lens placed in the 1870 tower (NPS). The USLHS gives 1857.
Small addition so the keeper could stay at the light in stormy weather.
32-foot fog-bell tower (LighthouseFriends). The NPS place page gives 1889 for the current tower.
Light moved onto the fog-bell tower; the 1870 tower was demolished.
Electric bell striker installed; fog bell sounds one blow every fifteen seconds.
Keeper Gary E. Powell transferred to Cedar Point Lighthouse.
Fort transferred to the Interior Department; the light station stayed under the Coast Guard.
Keepers ended; light changed to an unmanned automatic flashing red light.
Tower turned over to the National Park Service, per LighthouseFriends. The NPS says in 1950 the tower was to stay with the Coast Guard; see resolved_conflicts.
Major restoration by the NPS Historic Preservation Training Center.
Coast Guard removed the light and the '80' daymark from the tower and moved the light to the river.

wrecks.vessel: gasoline boat M-212, U.S. Army Quartermaster Department
wrecks.outcome: Sank in the Potomac. Keeper Gary E. Powell rendered assistance to the boat and its two occupants; Secretary Hoover commended him (Bulletin 1922).
Ran onto submerged piling near the fort; Keeper Powell assisted in floating her (Commissioner's report; the printed item gives no day).

corrections.why: The Coast Guard removed the light from the tower in 2020 (NPS; LighthouseFriends), and the record's own events list a 2020 deactivation. Confirm against the current Coast Guard light list whether the river light is still a separate aid under this LLNR.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends dates the 32-foot fog-bell tower to 1882. The USCG Historian's page, seen only as a search snippet, also gives 1882; the page itself was not read. The NPS place page says the current tower was built in 1889. Not resolved; the story gives both.
The USLHS archive gives the sixth-order lens for 1857. The NPS puts it in the 1870 tower, and LighthouseFriends describes the 1870 tower without naming a lens. Not resolved.

LighthouseFriends says the tower was turned over to the NPS in 2005. The NPS 1950 recommendation (as printed on its page) said the Coast Guard would keep the tower. The NPS place page does not say who owns it now.
The record says active. NPS and LighthouseFriends say the light was removed from the tower in 2020. The record's own event list has the 2020 deactivation (Rowlett).

notes_for_editor: Confidence is medium. Several dates disagree and are reported in resolved_conflicts. The Lighthouse Service Bulletin 1922 OCR reads 'Gary F. Powell'; the roster and the Commissioner's report say 'Gary E. Powell', and the story uses E. The OCR reads the boat 'M-21!2'; the story does not give the number. The wreck entry uses M-212 as the likely reading. The 1900 Light-House Board passage (item 609) is cited by scan page 114; the printed page was not read. The 1896-1897 Light-House Board passage (item 528) is cited to the bound volume; its scan page was not read. The Commissioner's 1915 to 1922 volume gives printed page 53 for the Lillian item, and the Bulletin's page 34 for the 1922 rescue. The roster runs to 1947 and 'Melvin S. Austin (1947-)' is open-ended; no keeper after 1947 is named in the story. Evening Times (Washington), 4 November 1901, prints a Fifth District appropriation list that includes a 'new tower' at Fort Washington at a garbled amount ('$1 60'). It is not used: the list does not say whether it was enacted. Chronicling America searches for 'Fort Washington light' in Washington papers 1899 to 1903 returned mostly advertisements. The USCG Historian's archived Fort Washington page returned HTTP 403 and was not read. The Wikipedia lead (1870 tower built in Baltimore; 1882 bell tower; 1901 move) was read for leads only and is not cited. Position: the record's OSM point (38.712276 N, 77.036897 W) and the USLHS position (38 42.42 N, 77 02.13 W) differ by about 0.6 km; no correction proposed.
